We set US=0 in all the trials of the probe phase.

To illustrate the predictions of the model in Figures 2E, F, 8D, we chose parameters that result in qualitatively similar effects to the experimental results. For both Experiments 1 and 2, we set λ to 15, similar to the observed implicit adaptation asymptotes in these experiments, as well as in other studies (Bond and Taylor, 2015; Morehead et al., 2017). The value of β was set to 0.12 (Experiment 1) or 0.02 (Experiment 4), the salience parameter (α) for the movement plan CS to 0.99, and both the tone CS and light CS to 0.002 (Experiment 1) or 0.1 (Experiment 4). These divergent salience values are consistent with the assumption that most of the associative strength of the US would be absorbed by the movement plan CS given its central relevance to the task of reaching to a target. The remainder of potential associative strength to the US is thus available for the tone and light CSs.

To demonstrate how the choice of parameters in the Rescorla-Wagner model influences the predicted Pavlovian effects, we simulated behavior using various combinations of the free parameters. We chose several combinations of values for β and λ, and, for each combination, a wide range of values for αgoal, αtone and αlight (For simplicity, we constrained αtone and αlight to the same value.). Figure 3 displays heatmaps resulting from these simulations, with the color of each cell corresponding to the simulated difference in the trial-by-trial change in heading angle between CS+ and CS− trials. In addition, we illustrated that a single-process state-space model, a standard model of sensorimotor adaptation, cannot capture these Pavlovian effects. In this model, the motor state is updated according to the error observed during the previous movement. The parameters of this model determine both the trial-by-trial retention of the previous motor state and the rate of learning from errors (see Equation 2 in the Results). For the simulation presented in Figure 3, the error was fixed to one of two values during the acquisition phase, either –15° on CS+ trials or 0° on CS− trials, and in the probe phase, it was set to 0° on all trials.

While the two models share similar features and parameters (e.g. learning rate of an error signal), the additional parameters in the Rescorla-Wagner model allow it to capture the effects of differential and compound conditioning, should these processes be operative in our experiments. For example, in the differential conditioning case, modifying the parameters of the Rescorla-Wagner model could produce changes in the magnitude of both the within-trial ‘Pavlovian’ effects (i.e. the modulation of behavior in response to the current CS, or ‘trial n’ effects) and across-trial adaptation effects (i.e. the modulation of behavior in response to the current state of learning, or ‘trial n−1’ effects). However, the Rescorla-Wagner model will always yield unique responses to the CS+ and CS− given non-zero salience parameters. In contrast, no combination of the A and B parameters in the state-space model will produce differential responses to the tone and light CSs.

To simulate the dynamics of the adaptation and Pavlovian effects in differential conditioning (Figure 5A) and to compare it to the dynamics observed in the actual data (Figure 5B), we simulated the trial-by-trial change in heading angle during acquisition (600 trials) according to the Rescorla-Wagner model (Equations 1; 3) and the state-space model (Equation 2.) based on the schedules of CS+ and CS− trials that were presented to the participants (16 simulated time courses). For the Rescorla-Wagner model, we used the same parameters values that generated the simulation results presented in Figure 2E and F. For the state-space model, we set the A parameter to 0.9 and B to 0.12. We then did the same trial-by-trial regression analysis described above for the actual heading angle data (see Data analysis) with the exception that the dependent variable was now the simulated change in heading angle.

### Model fitting and comparison

We conducted a post-hoc model comparison analysis (Figure 4). In this analysis, we fit the Rescorla-Wagner model (Equations 1; 3) and the standard state-space model (Equation 2) to participants’ heading angle time course data of Experiment 1. The two models were fit by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between the measured and modeled movement data, using the MATLAB function fmincon. To avoid local minima, 200 randomized sets of initial parameter values were used during fitting, and the best fit of each model was selected for model comparison. Models were compared using both the sum of squared residuals and the AIC approximated on the residuals (Akaike, 1974). All free parameters were bound at (0, 1), except for λ, which was bounded at (–30, 60). We did not perform model fitting for Experiment 4 since all trials were identical in the acquisition phase. As such, the salience parameters in the Rescorla-Wagner model for the goal, tone, and light are unidentifiable, and both models make indistinguishable behavioral predictions during acquisition.

This paper provides a fundamental account of the role associative learning plays in sensorimotor adaptation. In a compelling result, the authors show that by pairing movement-related feedback with conditioning cues in the form of neutral auditory or visual contextual cues can be used to differentiate between sensorimotor perturbations/states. This work nicely integrates multiple literatures surrounding the processes supported by the cerebellum and solves a long-standing puzzle of exactly how and when arbitrary cues can serve to shape motor adaptation.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Contextual effects in sensorimotor adaptation adhere to associative learning rules" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Michael Frank as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) More evidence for the temporal specificity of results. The authors advance the idea that the key difference between the current results and previous work that has failed to find evidence of associative learning is the temporal relationship between cues and feedback. However, no experimental evidence is provided that this timing is fundamental. There is a need for new data showing the importance of the temporal relationship to support many of the conclusions drawn in the article. (See comments from reviewer 2 below.)

2) There are many instances of places in the manuscript that lacked clarity and could benefit from more exposition and inclusion of some of the supplementary analyses. These include a better explanation of the task, how the various stimuli (US, CS, etc) map onto the task, the inclusion of Supp. Figure 1 in the main text, and (See comments from both reviewers below.)

3) More discussion about the models considered and their similarities/differences and their diverging predictions.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I recommend writing a clearer explanation of the associative learning approach investigated here and the relationship between standard ways of looking at visuomotor rotation and associative learning and making the notation for the latter clear and concise

I suspect some of the readers of this article will be more familiar with VR rotation and dynamic learning as less so with classical conditioning. The task could certainly be explained more clearly.

It would help to have a more explanation of how the current study operates as a standard visuo motor rotation task. Then explain how this is related to a classical conditioning task. There are lots of abbreviations including CS+, CS- etc. it would be helpful to have a table to illustrate the analogous link between conditioning and VR learning.

Figure 1 could be explained better. Suggest having a bigger schematic of the task since understanding this is key to understanding the article. maybe have it as a single figure

Simulations of the RW models are carried out. However only their basic formulas are stated (Equations 1 and 2). It would be better to show more details in the methods (by providing the equations) for how precisely experiments 1 and 2 were simulated. pseudocode for explaining simulations would also be nice.

There is a mention of simple state space models not being able to deal with contextual effects. It would be useful to elaborate on this with reference to the equations that describe these models. It would also be helpful to discuss the differences between RW model and state space models, And also the deficiencies of both.

Supplementary figures are used. I would suggest it's better to fully explain them and include them as part of the main document.

The Github supplementary materials appears to be a clone of the author's working directory for simulations of this project and it is also hard to follow. There is of course no need for all this detail, but it's fine to provide it. I would however suggest that the main scripts for critical simulations for Experiments 1 and 2 are made easy to identify and run, if readers wish to do so.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

Temporal specificity of results: The authors predict and conclude that the key parameter for observing associative learning when using arbitrary stimuli as contextual cues is the temporal relationship of these cues to the feedback. They provide compelling evidence of associative learning however at present provide no evidence of the importance of this temporal relationship. Considering this is assumed to be the key difference between the current results and previous work who have failed to find an effect, I believe the article requires additional work (maybe by introducing a delay between CS and movement) that examines the importance of this temporal relationship. Providing evidence that the associative learning effect is dependent on the timing between the cue and feedback being between 100-500ms is fundamental to support some conclusions made in the article.

Exp 1 probe phase results: Whilst not significant (n-1 x n interaction), there seemed to be a clear difference between CS+ trials within the different trial n-1 contexts (Figure 1D). In fact, this difference seems bigger (and as consistent) as the meaningful/significant differences which are focused on. Interestingly, the RW model predicts a clear n-1 x n interaction however it is not discussed why (Figure 1F). To me it seems that the behaviour (at least partially) and model reflect an interaction between trial n-1 and n during probe trials however this is currently not discussed. Could the authors elaborate on this result and include this in the article?

Magnitude of effect (supplementary S1 figure): Suppl Figure 1 needs to be in the main article as it provides context and some 'raw' data. It would also be beneficial to have in the main article a similar figure but with the CS+ and CS- trial types separated. Suppl Figure 1 is important as it highlights that the conditioning effects are relatively small. This needs to be explained/mentioned in the results i.e., that the differences between CS+ vs CS- (1-degree) are approx. 6% of the total adaptation that occurred (15-degrees). I suppose this is referred to within the final exp 1 analysis (Figure 2B) but its not explicit. Although I believe the results are important, the article currently reads as if these conditioning effects were large when in fact other people might conclude that conditioning had little impact on adaptation (as similar adaptation (approx. 15-degrees) was observed across both contexts (assumed as this is not shown) and performance looks very similar to exp 2 where there was no 0-degree context). There needs to be some acknowledgement of the fact that while these conditioning effects appear meaningful, they were small (with most participants showing less than a 1-degree difference between contexts).

Exp 2 results: It was unclear to me why the RW model would predict a negative heading angle within the single CS conditions (Figure 3C)? I understand that a weaker conditioning response would be expected due to compound conditioning, but would you not expect this still to be positive? Why would the model predict extinction to occur and why is this seen in the behaviour? The details of this result (and the predictions of the model) are currently not discussed in sufficient/any detail.

What is the CS (confusion between results and discussion)? Between lines 395-410 the authors describe the primary CS as being the heading angle ('the movement plan itself, rather than the target cue, that constitutes the primary CS'), however in the results (lines 74-96) they describe the CS as being the arbitrary cue ('When considered through the lens of classical conditioning, the arbitrary cues are the conditioned stimuli (CSs)') and the CR being the heading angle ('the conditioned response (CR) would be the movement heading angle elicited by a CS'). As a result of this discrepancy, I found this section of the discussion very confusing (lines 387-410 and then again from line 433). Are the authors saying that sometimes the heading angle/plan is the CS and other times it is the CR…? How does this all align? One can see why a suggestion for a figure showing this mechanism visually is suggested below.

Link between this work and recent contextual inference model by Heald et al.,: Could the authors provide a more direct comparison between the current work and the contextual inference model by Heald et al., (in discussion)? The authors currently say 'their model suggests that spontaneous recovery and consistency effects emerge due to contextual inferences that likely interact with deliberate changes in explicit strategies' however does this align with the current work? How does contextual inference align/differ with these conditioning mechanisms? In future work, the authors seem to want to explain the phenomena (spontaneous recovery etc) recently explained by this model and I am interested to know whether these are competing explanations or are explaining the same mechanism or are different but complementary?

Use of supplementary figures: Why did the authors decide to put so much of the important detail into the supplementary? In my opinion, all of this should be in the main article.

Normality of data and presentation of individual data: There is no mention of any assessment of data normality, was the data normally distributed? In addition, a greater amount of individual data should be shown rather than mean +- SEM.

Figure to represent conditioning mechanism: I would find it very helpful if an additional figure was added which showed the US, UR, CS and CR visually. I kept forgetting how each of them were proposed to be represented in the task.

claims.claim: Participants showed a robust adaptation effect during the acquisition phase of Experiment 1.
claims.source: There was a robust adaptation effect (Figure 2C, left panel). Trial-by-trial changes in reaching direction (Δ heading angle) were significantly affected by the CS presented on the previous trial (F[1, 15]=13.4, p=0.002, BF10=41.45, and ηp2=0.47) such that the change in heading angle was larger after CS+ trials compared to after CS− trials (mean difference: 1.50°, 95% CI: [0.70° 2.30°]).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and Figure 2C

claims.claim: The change in heading angle was larger after CS+ trials compared to after CS− trials in Experiment 1 acquisition phase (mean difference: 1.50°, 95% CI: [0.70° 2.30°]).
claims.source: Trial-by-trial changes in reaching direction (Δ heading angle) were significantly affected by the CS presented on the previous trial (F[1, 15]=13.4, p=0.002, BF10=41.45, and ηp2=0.47) such that the change in heading angle was larger after CS+ trials compared to after CS− trials (mean difference: 1.50°, 95% CI: [0.70° 2.30°]).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: A clear Pavlovian effect was observed during the acquisition phase of Experiment 1.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2C (both panels), the results revealed clear Pavlovian effects during the acquisition phase. The heading angle increased in the direction of adaptation on CS+ trials (i.e. a positive change in heading angle relative to previous trials) and decreased on CS− trials (mean difference: 0.82°, 95% CI: [0.13° 1.51°]; F[1, 15]=5.37, p=0.035, BF10=2.89, and ηp2=0.26).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and Figure 2C

claims.claim: The heading angle increased on CS+ trials and decreased on CS− trials during acquisition in Experiment 1 (mean difference: 0.82°, 95% CI: [0.13° 1.51°]).
claims.source: The heading angle increased in the direction of adaptation on CS+ trials (i.e. a positive change in heading angle relative to previous trials) and decreased on CS− trials (mean difference: 0.82°, 95% CI: [0.13° 1.51°]; F[1, 15]=5.37, p=0.035, BF10=2.89, and ηp2=0.26).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: An interaction was observed between CS identity on trials n−1 and n in Experiment 1 acquisition phase.
claims.source: We also observed an interaction between CS identity on trials n−1 and n (F[1, 15]=4.70, p=0.047, BF10=2.21, and ηp2=0.24). That is, the difference between CS+ and CS− was larger on trials following a CS− (mean: 1.05°, 95% CI: [0.20° 1.89°]) compared to trials following a CS+ (0.58°, [–0.13° 1.30°]).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: The results of Experiment 1 appear to pertain exclusively to feedforward learning.

claims.claim: A clear Pavlovian effect was observed during the probe phase of Experiment 1.
claims.source: Here too, we observed a clear Pavlovian effect. claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and Figure 2D

claims.claim: There was a significant main effect of the CS on trial n during the probe phase of Experiment 1 (1.06°, [0.53° 1.59°]).

claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: The Pavlovian effect was not driven by explicit awareness of the CS-US contingency in Experiment 1.
claims.source: The Pavlovian effect did not appear to be driven by explicit awareness of the CS-US contingency. A post-experiment survey was used to classify participants as either aware or unaware of the CS-US associations (see Materials and methods). Participants who reported being aware of the contingencies (N=7) did not show a different Pavlovian effect compared to those who reported being unaware (N=9) in either the acquisition (–0.34°, [–1.90° 1.22°]; t[14]=−0.470, p=0.647, BF10=0.46, and d=−0.24) or probe (–0.14°, [–1.34° 1.07°]; t[14]=−0.242, p=0.813, BF10=0.44, and d=−0.12) phases.
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing aware and unaware participants

claims.claim: The Rescorla-Wagner model can capture differential conditioning behavior similar to the results observed in Experiment 1.
claims.source: To examine whether the Rescorla-Wagner model can capture differential conditioning behavior similar to the results observed in Experiment 1, we performed model simulations. The simulation results demonstrated both the adaptation effect and Pavlovian effect for the acquisition phase (Figure 2E), as well as a clear Pavlovian effect for the probe phase (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figures 2E and 2F

claims.claim: The behavioral signature of differential conditioning holds for essentially all combinations of parameters in the Rescorla-Wagner model.
claims.source: Importantly, the behavioral signature of differential conditioning – the larger changes in heading angle on CS+ trials compared to CS− trials – holds for essentially all combinations of parameters in the Rescorla-Wagner model (Figure 3, left side).
claims.evidence: Supported by parameter space simulations shown in Figure 3

claims.claim: The basic state-space model is unable to account for context effects in sensorimotor adaptation.
claims.source: However, the basic state-space model is unable to account for context effects. Unlike the Rescorla-Wagner model, it does not include parameters that allow the updating of separate states that are associated with distinct contexts. It predicts the change in behavior based on the outcome of the previous trial (i.e. the adaptation effect); it cannot account for variation in heading angle due to the CS on the current trial (i.e. the Pavlovian effect; Figure 3, right side).
claims.evidence: Supported by model simulations and theoretical analysis shown in Figure 3

claims.claim: The Rescorla-Wagner model provided a better fit to the data than a standard state-space model in Experiment 1.
claims.source: The Rescorla-Wagner model provided a better fit to the data than a standard state-space model, underscoring the significant role of the Pavlovian effect (Figure 4; t test comparing sum of squared residuals, –6.61×104, [–1.05×105 –2.72×104]; t[15]=–3.62, p=0.003, and d=−0.90; t test comparing Akaike information criterion (AIC) values, –430, [–572 –288]; t[15]=–6.44, p<0.001, and d=−1.61).
claims.evidence: Supported by model comparison analysis shown in Figure 4

claims.claim: At early stages of acquisition in Experiment 1, the adaptation effect emerged rapidly while the Pavlovian effect was small.
claims.source: As expected, at early stages of acquisition, the adaptation effect emerged rapidly, whereas the contribution of the Pavlovian effect was small.
claims.evidence: Supported by time course analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: Over experience in Experiment 1, the relative contribution of the adaptation and Pavlovian effects reversed.
claims.source: Over experience, the relative contribution of the two effects reversed (type X time bin interaction effect: F[1, 365]=16.7, p<0.001). The Pavlovian effect gradually grew (mean slope: 0.14, 95% CI: [0.04 0.24]) at the expense of the adaptation effect, which eventually exhibited a reduced contribution (–0.15, [–0.25 –0.05]; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis and Figure 5B

claims.claim: The Pavlovian effect gradually grew over experience in Experiment 1 (mean slope: 0.14, 95% CI: [0.04 0.24]).
claims.source: The Pavlovian effect gradually grew (mean slope: 0.14, 95% CI: [0.04 0.24])
claims.evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis

claims.claim: The adaptation effect exhibited a reduced contribution over experience in Experiment 1 (–0.15, [–0.25 –0.05]).
claims.source: at the expense of the adaptation effect, which eventually exhibited a reduced contribution (–0.15, [–0.25 –0.05]; Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis

claims.claim: Extending the CS-US interval by approximately 1000 ms rendered arbitrary sensory contextual cues ineffective in separating distinct motor memories.
claims.source: These results suggest that extending the CS-US interval by approximately 1000 ms rendered arbitrary sensory contextual cues ineffective in separating distinct motor memories.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the results of Experiment 2

claims.claim: During the acquisition phase of Experiment 2, participants exhibited a marked change in movement direction with a mean asymptote of ~25°.
claims.source: During the acquisition phase of Experiment 2, participants exhibited a marked change in movement direction, opposite to the direction of the clamped feedback (adaptation effect: F[1, 63]=47.3, p<0.001, BF10=7.58×106, ηp2=0.43, mean difference, 95% CI; 1.80°, [1.29° 2.31°]), reaching a mean asymptote of ~25° (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 6B

claims.claim: A Pavlovian differential conditioning effect was not detected during the acquisition phase of Experiment 2.
claims.source: Despite this increase in overall adaptation, a Pavlovian differential conditioning effect was not detected (F[1, 63]=0.54, p=0.465, BF10=0.16, ηp2=0.01, mean difference: 0.17°, 95% CI: [–0.29° 0.63°])
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: No reliable Pavlovian effect was found during the probe phase of Experiment 2.
claims.source: Importantly, and consistent with the results from the acquisition phase, we again found no reliable Pavlovian effect (F[1, 63]=1.36, p=0.248, BF10=0.25, ηp2=0.02, mean difference: 0.28°, 95% CI: [–0.19° 0.75°])

claims.claim: A significant Pavlovian effect was observed during the acquisition phase of Experiment 3.
claims.source: However, unlike Experiment 2, we now observed a significant Pavlovian effect (F[1, 63]=6.05, p=0.017, BF10=2.35, ηp2=0.09, mean difference, 95% CI; 0.34°, [0.07° 0.61°]; Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and Figure 7C

claims.claim: The Pavlovian effect was significant in the probe phase of Experiment 3.

claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: The efficacy of arbitrary stimuli in serving as contextual cues for sensorimotor conditioning is subject to strong temporal constraints.
claims.source: Taken together, the results of Experiments 2 and 3 support our conjecture that the efficacy of arbitrary stimuli in serving as contextual cues for sensorimotor conditioning is subject to strong temporal constraints, a key feature of cerebellar-dependent learning.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combined results of Experiments 2 and 3

claims.claim: Arbitrary stimuli proved effective for differential conditioning when the CS-US interval was short (around 300 ms) but not when the interval was extended (around 1000 ms).
claims.source: Even when the tone and light no longer required attention, they proved effective for differential conditioning when the interval between these CSs and the US was short (around 300 ms) but not when the interval was extended (around 1000 ms).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of results from Experiments 2 and 3

claims.claim: The additivity principle is based on the idea that there is an associative capacity for a given US.
claims.source: This principle is based on the idea that there is an associative capacity for a given US – the V term in the Rescorla-Wagner equation. That is, multiple CSs can become associated with a given US, but the combined associative strength is bounded by V.
claims.evidence: Supported by established theory in associative learning

claims.claim: CSs effectively compete with one another due to the capacity constraint on associative strength.
claims.source: As a result of this capacity constraint, CSs effectively compete with one another, with the associative strength split among multiple cues.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the additivity principle

claims.claim: The additivity principle has received ample support in behavioral and neural studies of associative learning.
claims.source: The additivity principle has received ample support in behavioral and neural studies of associative learning (Giurfa, 2007; Kehoe et al., 1994; Kehoe and Schreurs, 1986; Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Weiss, 1972)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claims.claim: Robust adaptation was observed in the acquisition phase of Experiment 4.
claims.source: As in Experiments 1–3, we again observed robust adaptation in the acquisition phase, manifesting as a change in heading angle in the direction opposite the clamp (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 8B

claims.source: We observed a significant Pavlovian effect of CS type on these no-feedback trials (Friedman test: χ2[2]=9.82, p=0.007, and W=0.223), with larger changes in heading angles on compound CS trials (median: 0.39°, interquartile range: [–0.05° 0.49°]) relative to the tone-alone (–0.15°, [–0.47° 0.18°], p=0.020) or light-alone (–0.22°, [–0.52° 0.34°]p=0.020) trials, conforming to the first prediction of the additivity principle (Figure 8C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and Figures 8C and 8D

claims.claim: Larger changes in heading angles were observed on compound CS trials relative to tone-alone or light-alone trials in Experiment 4 probe phase.
claims.source: with larger changes in heading angles on compound CS trials (median: 0.39°, interquartile range: [–0.05° 0.49°]) relative to the tone-alone (–0.15°, [–0.47° 0.18°], p=0.020) or light-alone (–0.22°, [–0.52° 0.34°]p=0.020) trials
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: Participants who were more sensitive to the tone stimulus were less sensitive to the light stimulus and vice versa in Experiment 4 (Pearson correlation: r=−0.72, p<0.001).
claims.source: Participants who were more sensitive to the tone stimulus were less sensitive to the light stimulus and vice versa (Figure 8E, Pearson correlation: r=−0.72, p<0.001, and BF10=163.2).
claims.evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claims.claim: The target can be viewed as a highly effective contextual cue in standard adaptation tasks.
claims.source: As such, a tight temporal link is established between target appearance and movement, echoing (perhaps inadvertently) the CS-US temporal constraints essential for cerebellar-dependent conditioning. Under these conditions, the target can be viewed as a highly effective contextual cue.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the temporal relationship between target appearance and movement

claims.claim: The movement plan itself constitutes the primary, strongest CS in sensorimotor adaptation.
claims.source: More precisely, we propose that it is the movement plan itself that constitutes the primary, strongest CS.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on theoretical considerations

claims.claim: Generalization of adaptation appears to be centered around the direction of the movement plan, not the target.
claims.source: First, generalization of adaptation appears to be centered around the direction of the movement plan, not the target (Day et al., 2016; McDougle et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claims.claim: The mere activation of different motor plans can serve as efficient contextual cues, negating interference effects from opposing perturbations.
claims.source: Second, even in the absence of distinct contextual movements (e.g. follow-throughs), the mere activation of different motor plans can serve as efficient contextual cues, negating interference effects from opposing perturbations (Sheahan et al., 2016; Sheahan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claims.claim: The prediction that constitutes the basis for the sensory prediction error is computed using an efference copy of the movement intention.
claims.source: Third, an emphasis on the movement plan is in accord with theoretical models of cerebellar-dependent adaptation, where the prediction that constitutes the basis for the sensory prediction error is computed using an efference copy of the movement intention (Blakemore et al., 2001; Gao et al., 2016; Kawato and Gomi, 1992; Kim et al., 2022; Wolpert et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claims.claim: Using a single target location allowed elimination of any temporal linkage between the onset of the target and the feedback.
claims.source: In addition, using a single target location allowed us to have the target remain on the screen throughout the entire experiment, eliminating any temporal linkage between the onset of the target and the feedback.
claims.evidence: Supported by the experimental design

claims.claim: There is considerable evidence demonstrating that the clamp method effectively isolates implicit adaptation.
claims.source: While a single target may facilitate the use of simple explicit strategies (McDougle and Taylor, 2019), empirically, there is considerable evidence demonstrating that the clamp method effectively isolates implicit adaptation (Morehead et al., 2017; Tsay et al., 2020c; Avraham et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claims.claim: The asymptotic values in Experiment 2 and 3 were higher than those seen in Experiment 1, possibly due to differences in the experimental setup.
claims.source: The asymptotic values in this experiment were higher than those seen in Experiment 1, possibly due to differences in the experimental setup (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: Observed in the data and speculated about the cause

claims.claim: Experiments 1 and 4 were conducted in the laboratory using a tablet and digitizing pen setup.
claims.source: Experiments 1 and 4 were conducted in our laboratory, using a tablet and digitizing pen setup in which the movements involve arm movements of at least 8 cm.
claims.evidence: Description of experimental methods

claims.claim: Experiments 2 and 3 were conducted via a web-based platform with participants using their personal computers.
claims.source: In contrast, Experiments 2 and 3 were conducted via a web-based platform, with each participant using their personal computer with a mouse or a trackpad to produce wrist or finger movements of ~2 cm (depending on the sensitivity of the device).
claims.evidence: Description of experimental methods

claims.claim: Basic phenomena of visuomotor adaptation are similar between lab- and web-based platforms.
claims.source: Although basic phenomena of visuomotor adaptation are similar between lab- and web-based platforms (Tsay et al., 2021), there may be mechanistic differences.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claims.claim: The laboratory setup may be better suited for providing reliable proprioceptive information, which may limit the extent of adaptation.
claims.source: We expect that the laboratory setup may be much better suited for providing reliable information concerning proprioception, information that may limit the extent of adaptation (Salomonczyk et al., 2011; Tsay et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Speculated based on cited research about proprioception

claims.claim: Proprioception may have a reduced effect in limiting adaptation in web-based studies, leading to a higher asymptote.
claims.source: Given that proprioceptive and visual signals are not aligned in the web-based studies, proprioception may have a reduced effect in limiting adaptation, leading to a higher asymptote.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on differences in experimental setup

claims.claim: The Rescorla-Wagner model was developed to account for phenomena such as differential conditioning and compound conditioning.
claims.source: The success of this model to capture the general features of the current datasets should not be surprising since the model was developed to account for phenomena such as differential conditioning and compound conditioning.
claims.evidence: Supported by knowledge of the model's history

claims.claim: It was overdetermined that the Rescorla-Wagner model would provide better fits than the standard state-space model given that the latter cannot capture contextual effects.
claims.source: Thus, it was somewhat overdetermined that the Rescorla-Wagner model would provide better fits than the standard state-space model in our study, given that the latter cannot capture contextual effects.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the limitations of the state-space model

claims.claim: To account for compound conditioning, a state-space model would essentially have to be transformed into a facsimile of a Rescorla-Wagner model.
claims.source: However, we emphasize that to account for compound conditioning, and in particular the additivity principle (i.e. overshadowing), a state-space model would essentially have to be transformed into a facsimile of a Rescorla-Wagner model, supporting our key conclusions.
claims.evidence: Inferred from theoretical considerations

claims.claim: Spontaneous recovery is the re-manifestation of a previously adapted state in the absence of error feedback.
claims.source: One such effect is spontaneous recovery, the re-manifestation of a previously adapted state in the absence of error feedback.
claims.evidence: Definition from the literature

claims.claim: A variant of the state-space model with multiple states with different learning and forgetting rates can capture spontaneous recovery.
claims.source: A variant of the state-space model, one that allows for multiple states with different learning and forgetting rates, can capture spontaneous recovery (Smith et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claims.claim: Learning is faster in response to a consistent vs inconsistent perturbation.
claims.source: A second example is the relationship between learning rate and environmental consistency; learning is faster in response to a consistent vs inconsistent perturbation (Albert et al., 2021; Avraham et al., 2020; Gonzalez Castro et al., 2014; Herzfeld et al., 2014; Hutter and Taylor, 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claims.claim: Savings refers to faster adaptation upon a second exposure to the same perturbation.
claims.source: A third example is savings upon relearning, where faster adaptation is observed upon a second exposure to the same perturbation (Huang et al., 2011; Krakauer et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claims.claim: Studies have modeled savings using multi-rate state-space models, learning rate modulation, or a combination of these factors.
claims.source: Studies have modeled savings using multi-rate state-space models (Smith et al., 2006), learning rate modulation (Herzfeld et al., 2014), or a combination of these factors (Zarahn et al., 2008; Mawase et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claims.claim: The COIN model posits that motor adaptation arises from two interacting mechanisms: proper learning and apparent learning.
claims.source: The contextual inference (COIN) model posits that motor adaptation arises from two interacting mechanisms: proper learning, which involves the creation and updating of context-specific memories, and apparent learning, a process of inferring the current context to determine which memory to express (recall).
claims.evidence: Description of the COIN model from the literature

claims.claim: The COIN model stresses the importance of the environment in guiding memory retrieval.
claims.source: Unlike conventional context-independent models of motor adaptation, the COIN model stresses the importance of the environment in guiding memory retrieval.
claims.evidence: Description of the COIN model from the literature

claims.claim: The implementation of the Rescorla-Wagner model in this study maps to the proper learning component of the COIN model.
claims.source: In one sense, our implementation of the Rescorla-Wagner model follows a similar philosophy. However, it maps to the proper learning component of the COIN model since we assume that the current context is determined by the actual properties of the environment in an all-or-none manner (e.g. the CS presented by the experimenter).
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of the models

claims.claim: The COIN model suggests that spontaneous recovery, consistency effects, and savings may emerge due to contextual inferences.
claims.source: The COIN model suggests that spontaneous recovery, consistency effects, and savings may emerge due to contextual inferences; these inferences likely involve cognitive systems related to executive function and non-motor memory systems (Collins and McDougle, 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to the COIN model literature

claims.claim: Growing evidence shows that spontaneous recovery, consistency effects, and savings are, in large degree, the result of strategic changes.
claims.source: Consistent with this view, growing evidence shows that these phenomena are, in large degree, the result of strategic changes (Haith et al., 2015; Morehead et al., 2015; Leow et al., 2020; Avraham et al., 2020; Avraham et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to recent research

claims.claim: The basic Rescorla-Wagner model is unable to account for higher order effects such as spontaneous recovery or savings.
claims.source: While the basic Rescorla-Wagner model is unable to account for higher order effects such as spontaneous recovery or savings, we envision that complimenting it with more sophisticated, Bayesian inference models could readily accommodate these phenomena.

results.result: Experiment 1 demonstrates that arbitrary sensory cues (tone and light) can act as effective contextual cues in sensorimotor adaptation when a strict temporal relationship (~300 ms CS-US interval) is established. Both adaptation effects (trial-to-trial learning from errors) and Pavlovian effects (differential responses to CS+ vs CS-) were observed during acquisition and probe phases, with the Pavlovian effect being independent of explicit awareness.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C28 provide converging statistical evidence for both adaptation and Pavlovian effects in Experiment 1. The data show significant differential conditioning (p=0.002 for adaptation effect, p=0.035 for Pavlovian effect during acquisition; p=0.001 for Pavlovian effect during probe), rapid movement times precluding online corrections (C21-C23), and independence from explicit awareness (C28). The experimental design with tight temporal coupling between CS and US is well-justified.

results.result: The Rescorla-Wagner model successfully captures the differential conditioning behavior observed in Experiment 1, providing better fits than the standard state-space model. Model simulations show that the Pavlovian effect holds across essentially all parameter combinations, and time-course analysis reveals that the Pavlovian effect gradually increases while the adaptation effect decreases over training.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C36 demonstrate strong model validation through simulations (C29-C30), formal model comparison showing superior fits (C32: p=0.003 for SSR, p<0.001 for AIC), and time-course dynamics consistent with associative learning principles (C34-C36: interaction F[1,365]=16.7, p<0.001). The state-space model's inability to capture contextual effects (C31) is theoretically sound and empirically demonstrated.

results.result: Experiment 2 demonstrates that extending the CS-US interval by approximately 1000 ms abolishes the Pavlovian differential conditioning effect, despite robust overall adaptation. This temporal constraint is a key feature linking sensorimotor adaptation to cerebellar-dependent associative learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 provide clear statistical evidence that while adaptation occurred (F[1,63]=47.3, p<0.001), no Pavlovian effect was detected during either acquisition (p=0.465) or probe (p=0.248) phases when the CS-US interval was extended. This null result, combined with the positive results from Experiments 1 and 3, strongly supports the temporal constraint hypothesis (C43-C44).

results.result: Experiment 3 shows that when the CS and imperative are presented simultaneously (short CS-US interval ~300 ms), significant Pavlovian effects are restored, confirming that temporal proximity rather than attentional demands determines the efficacy of arbitrary cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 demonstrate significant Pavlovian effects during both acquisition (F[1,63]=6.05, p=0.017) and probe (F[1,63]=25.6, p<0.001) phases when temporal constraints are met. The comparison across Experiments 2 and 3 (C43-C44) provides strong evidence for temporal constraints, as the only difference was CS-US timing while attentional demands remained constant.

results.result: Experiment 4 demonstrates that sensorimotor adaptation adheres to the additivity principle of associative learning through compound conditioning. Participants showed stronger responses to compound CS trials than to individual CS elements, and a robust negative correlation (r=-0.72, p<0.001) between responses to the two elemental CSs, consistent with competitive cue interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 provide strong statistical evidence for compound conditioning effects (Friedman test: χ²[2]=9.82, p=0.007) and the critical negative correlation between elemental CS responses (C51-C52: r=-0.72, p<0.001, BF10=163.2). This overshadowing effect is a hallmark prediction of the additivity principle (C45-C47) and represents novel evidence linking sensorimotor adaptation to associative learning principles.

results.result: Both delay eyeblink conditioning and sensorimotor adaptation are cerebellar-dependent forms of learning, with eyeblink conditioning requiring close temporal proximity (100-500 ms) between CS and US for optimal learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by established literature on cerebellar function in both learning paradigms. Claims C6 and C15 regarding temporal constraints in eyeblink conditioning are supported by classic citations (Schneiderman and Gormezano, 1964; Smith et al., 1969). These provide the theoretical foundation for the experimental hypotheses.

results.result: Prior research shows that movement-related contextual cues are highly effective for separating motor memories, while arbitrary contextual cues (e.g., color) generally show large interference and are ineffective for defining distinct motor memories.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. This establishes the paradox that motivates the current study: why arbitrary cues fail in typical adaptation paradigms but succeed in eyeblink conditioning. The characterization of prior work appears accurate based on the cited studies.

results.result: The movement plan itself, rather than the target, constitutes the primary CS in sensorimotor adaptation. This is supported by evidence that generalization centers on movement direction, different motor plans serve as efficient contextual cues, and theoretical models use efference copies of movement intention for prediction.
results.evaluation: While claims C59-C61 cite supporting evidence, claim C58 is explicitly speculative. The experimental design (C62) eliminates temporal linkage between target onset and feedback, but this doesn't directly test whether the movement plan is the primary CS. Claims C59-C61 provide indirect support through cited literature, but the core proposal (C58) remains a theoretical interpretation rather than a directly tested hypothesis in this study.

results.result: Asymptotic adaptation values differed between lab-based (Experiments 1, 4: ~15°) and web-based (Experiments 2, 3: ~25°) platforms, possibly due to differences in proprioceptive reliability, with web-based setups potentially providing less reliable proprioceptive information that normally limits adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 accurately describe observed differences and methodological variations. However, the explanation (C68-C69) is explicitly speculative. While C67 cites evidence that basic phenomena are similar across platforms, the mechanistic explanation for the asymptote differences lacks direct empirical support. The speculation is reasonable but unvalidated, and alternative explanations (e.g., differences in movement scale, effector systems) are not ruled out.

results.result: The Rescorla-Wagner model's superior fit compared to the state-space model was somewhat overdetermined given that the state-space model cannot capture contextual effects. However, to account for compound conditioning and the additivity principle, a state-space model would need to be transformed into a facsimile of the Rescorla-Wagner model.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 provide appropriate caveats about model comparison. The acknowledgment that the comparison was "overdetermined" (C71) is intellectually honest given the state-space model's structural limitations. Claim C72 makes a valid theoretical point about what modifications would be required, supporting the key conclusions despite the limitations of the comparison.

results.result: The basic Rescorla-Wagner model cannot account for higher-order phenomena like spontaneous recovery, consistency effects, and savings, which may involve strategic processes and contextual inference. However, combining associative mechanisms with Bayesian inference models could accommodate these phenomena and provide a more comprehensive framework for sensorimotor adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C82 accurately characterize limitations of the basic model and cite appropriate literature on alternative explanations for higher-order phenomena. Claim C83 appropriately acknowledges the model's limitations. Claims C84-C85 propose reasonable future directions supported by citations to successful hybrid models in other domains. The evaluation is balanced and appropriately speculative about future work.

results.result: While the study demonstrates that core constraints of delay eyeblink conditioning are relevant for sensorimotor adaptation, it does not address the error-correction algorithm itself. Associative learning alone does not provide a mechanism for error correction, though speculatively, adaptation might operate as a lookup table of context-outcome associations rather than through forward models.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C91 provide appropriate scope limitations and acknowledge what the study does not address. The distinction between associative learning principles and error-correction mechanisms (C89-C91) is valid. Claims C92-C93 are explicitly speculative but represent reasonable alternative hypotheses for future investigation. The evaluation appropriately distinguishes between demonstrated findings and speculative implications.

results.result: Participants exhibited rapid response times (mean 293±49.0 ms) and movement times (103±31.2 ms) in Experiment 1, with no significant online corrections during movement, indicating that results pertain exclusively to feedforward learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C21-C22 provide clear empirical evidence for rapid movements and absence of online corrections (no difference in heading angle change: p=0.640, d=-0.12). The analysis comparing heading angles at different time points (C22) appropriately tests and rules out the online correction hypothesis. Claim C23's inference is well-supported by the data.

results.result: A total of 166 healthy volunteers participated across four experiments, with all participants in lab-based experiments being right-handed. The protocol was approved by the UC Berkeley IRB.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 provide standard methodological information about participants and ethical approval. The information is clearly stated and appropriate for the study design. No concerns about participant selection or ethical procedures are evident.
